title: Turmeric, Cumin and Coriander: The Ancient Trio Behind India's Lentils and Curries
excerpt: The centuries-old foundation of Indian cooking is three everyday spices — and the Ayurvedic logic of warming and cooling that makes them work together.
body:
• The "blend" is a foundational trio, not a pre-mixed masala: turmeric, cumin, and coriander — three spices that have anchored Indian cooking for centuries, grounded in the 5,000-year-old Ayurvedic tradition.
  • Each spice has a role: turmeric is warming and anti-inflammatory; cumin is heating, detoxifying, and good for skin; coriander seed is cooling, sweet, and bitter — deliberately paired to restore balance.
  • The technique that unlocks them is tadka — blooming spices in hot oil or ghee. Whole seeds (cumin, coriander) go in first; ground spices (turmeric) follow, so nothing scorches.
  • Try it tonight: for one pound of lentils, vegetables, or grains, use 2 teaspoons each of cumin and coriander seeds (or 1.5 teaspoons ground) plus 1 teaspoon ground turmeric, bloomed in ghee or a high-smoke-point oil.

The most powerful spice blend in Indian cooking isn't a blend at all — it's three spices you probably already own. Turmeric, cumin, and coriander form the foundation of countless dals, sabzis, and grain dishes, and their staying power is no accident: the trio is rooted in Ayurveda, the 5,000-year-old Indian system of holistic health, where food is medicine and digestion is everything.

"Everything we do, whether it's what we eat or how we live our lives, is intended to support our digestion," says Kaveri Datta Barros, an Ayurvedic health counselor and chef instructor. In Ayurveda — from the Sanskrit for "knowledge of life" — six tastes (sweet, sour, salty, pungent, astringent, bitter) work together to stoke the digestive fire, or agni. The turmeric-cumin-coriander trio is built on that logic: warming spices paired with a cooling one, so the dish lands in balance.

What each spice brings

Turmeric, the knobby rhizome related to ginger, is ground into a pungent, astringent, bitter powder with a peppery aroma. In Ayurveda it is considered a warming spice and an anti-inflammatory — and it gives golden milk, biryani, and countless curries their signature hue.

Cumin shares turmeric's pungent, bitter, astringent qualities but adds earthy depth. It is, in Barros's words, "heating, detoxifying, and good for skin." Coriander seed — from the same plant as cilantro — brings a citrusy, herbal note and is "cooling, sweet, and bitter." That cooling quality is the point: paired deliberately with the warming turmeric and cumin, coriander restores the balance the system demands.

The technique: tadka

The trio's power is unlocked by tadka — the Hindi term for blooming spices in hot oil or ghee. Heating spices in fat converts their fat-soluble flavor compounds from solid to liquid, helping them disperse evenly through the dish, deepen in flavor, and become easier to digest and absorb.

Order matters. Whole seeds and large spices — cumin and coriander seeds, cinnamon sticks, cardamom pods — go into the hot fat first. Ground spices like turmeric follow, since they scorch in seconds. The practical ratio: for one pound of lentils, vegetables, or grains, use 2 teaspoons each of cumin and coriander seeds (or 1.5 teaspoons ground), 1 teaspoon of ground turmeric, and a fat with a high smoke point — ghee, avocado oil, or untoasted sesame oil.

"Everything we do, whether it's what we eat or how we live our lives, is intended to support our digestion."

— Kaveri Datta Barros, Ayurvedic health counselor and chef instructor

Legumes need the full treatment

For dals and beans, Barros has a three-word rule: "soak, spice, and oil!" Lentils should soak 30 to 60 minutes (larger beans longer), and they should be cooked with generous fat, since legumes are naturally drying and astringent. Many lentil dishes are finished with a shower of fresh cilantro — which doubles down on coriander's cooling role.

Why it works abroad, too

For the diaspora kitchen, the trio's appeal is practical as much as philosophical: turmeric, cumin, and coriander are cheap, available in any Indian grocery store from Edison to Wembley, and shelf-stable for months. One small jar of each covers the flavor base of a week of meals — a centuries-old shortcut that still beats any pre-mixed masala for control. The result, as the tradition promises, is food that is deeply flavorful, nourishing, and easy to digest — the balance of warming and cooling doing the quiet work underneath.
